utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we proceed with this morning's evidence, we would like to briefly go into private session to deal with one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness proposed this morning, Dr. Baccard, has led to the submission by counsel for Mr. Lukic of a motion to exclude the testimony of the witness and the documentary evidence that goes beyond the scope of the indictment, and four particular areas are identified in the motion. The Prosecution were given an opportunity, if they wished, to file a written response to this before we started this morning and, I understand, decided to file no response. That doesn't necessarily complete the matter, Mr. Stamp. Is there anything you want to say about the motion to the effect that four of the areas addressed on the face of it by Dr. Baccard are not relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not object to the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's quite easy to identify the documents. It's a bit more difficult to deal with the testimony. And what I propose we do is in the next day or so identify the passages. Now, that could probably be done by agreement, and you could identify the passages and clarify for us for sure the documents, although I think they're easier for us to identify. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that can be done, Your Honour. Unfortunately, I also have another matter to raise, because in looking through the underlying material I discovered that one exhibit, in particular P206, also had an additional four sites that were the subject of some forensic examination for which there is evidence, allegations, et cetera, in the underlying material relating to Brusnik, Nevoljane, Skenderaj Srbica, and Mitrovica Sovido. These were not in my motion but these are also sites that are not ones for which we have had any pleadings in the indictment or any witnesses led about the underlying events. So in all fairness, I think I would have to let the Prosecution know that I consider these to also be ones that need to be excluded. And, again, I've so far been able to figure out which document it's related to and I think Mr. Stamp and I could come to a consensus as to what parts of the testimony might relate to that. We might be able to avoid even leading such evidence, either in cross or in direct, if that's the ruling of the Court. So that can be done, I think, and then -- well, I think I'll stop there and we'll finish this area because I have two other areas that are on a related but different theme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume that the written motion was the extent of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was until I had some more time to consult with my colleagues and to look through some of the other underlying materials, and there's a couple more technical objections. I could go into them very briefly now if that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the one you've just mentioned. It sounds, Mr. Stamp, as though you're only now being alerted to this additional contention that part of P206 relates to four additional areas which don't feature in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to deal with that straight off?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We won't be relying on that part of the exhibits. Some of the forensic teams examined many sites and they've prepared single reports for all the sites, and sometimes it included one or two other sites which are relevant. But we're not relying on the other sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ivetic, the other point you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The first point relates to exhibits -- parts of exhibits P206, P207, and P208, and I could identify them rather specifically if need be. Essentially, they relate to the beginning of each section on the various sites that are alleged in the indictment. It has a section entitled "The Facts" which essentially, from a reading of it, recite a version of the events as told or asserted by the investigators of the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, to the various forensic teams that worked there. And in the view of myself and at least one colleague who talked about this in considerable detail with me, we believe that this is an improper use of, in this instance, Rule 94 bis, to bring in the assertions of the OTP investigators and have them in the form of a written evidence as to what happened at the underlying sites where the forensic examinations or investigations were undertaken. We think it's an impermissible inference on the part of the written evidence to bring this in in this manner, especially since we don't know exactly what the bases or background is for the assertions that the investigators of the OTP make for the allegations. I mean, we can assume it's, in part, the witnesses we've heard, but it might also be the witnesses we have not heard for whatever reason. So we think that the section in each of the forensic investigations that gives a background of the facts ought not to come into the record or either be by redaction or by a ruling from the Court, that it will not considered or relied upon. I think that will also be sufficient, but I think we do need, for the record, to clarify that because it is in there and it is essentially something that OTP investigators are telling persons and for which the forensic investigators, apparently from the written material, have not undertaken any steps to verify, double-check, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure, if I can just open up my packet. For instance, in P206, beginning with the Izbica site, I believe it starts at page 5. The first paragraph says: "According to information provided by the ICTY investigators on 27 March 1999, the forces of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia attacked the village of Izbica and rounded up approximately 150 people who were then shot dead at three execution sites in the area around the village. Over the course of the next few days the victims were identified and buried in a field by villagers who survived. After the world press found out about the massacre, Serbian forces exhumed the bodies and transferred them to an unknown destination." That's the first site listed in P206 and it's submitted that this portion of the report is clearly just related to matters asserted by the ICTY investigators. In fact, when one reads the report, obviously there's parts of it that do not confirm the number of persons, et cetera, and it's obvious that this portion of the report is not based upon any forensic or scientific investigation that was undertaken and is merely a re-telling of what the Prosecution has alleged. So we just want to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, what's raised now is statements which are an introductory narrative to pathological findings which are specifically said to be matters asserted by ICTY investigators. What's your response to the suggestion that while these can be read as background introducing the rest of the material within each exhibit, these statements by ICTY investigators should not be considered to be evidence in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I entirely agree with that. It's the standard thing that forensic scientists, pathologists, will get a history of in respect of a body or the circumstances. It's just context in which the report was made and the examinations were done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you can take it, Mr. Ivetic, that the Trial Chamber is capable of distinguishing these statements from, for example, the hearsay investigation by the pathologist that might have led to the identification of the body through, for example, looking at associated documents, that sort of thing. Where it's clearly a statement of background history made by an investigator to identify the subject of the inquiry, then we will treat it as such and not as evidence per se in the case. For the avoidance of doubt, we shall order the Prosecution and the Lukic team, by close of business on Wednesday, so by the end of Wednesday, to submit an agreed statement of the passages in the -- this must be the transcript, I think, of Mr. Baccard -- Dr. Baccard from the previous case and the parts of the documentation that should not be considered by the Trial Chamber. Now, does that resolve the preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just one brief again which is with respect to P210 which falls in a different category. P210 is labelled as an expert ballistics report which talks about a wide variety of weapons and, in addition to giving technical information about the weapons, has peppered throughout it certain inferences, such as "this weapon is no longer -- is rarely used by regular units; nevertheless, the large number of them in circulation means it is possible to equip irregular units, such as paramilitaries, in a very short time. It was more than likely used in the theatre of operations." First of all, the witness that will be before us, Dr. Baccard, has a specific area of specialty, specific area of expert testimony that has been proposed. This expert ballistics report, I believe, goes beyond that where they're talking about weapons that, at least from my reading of the report, there is no indication of any forensic evidence that they were actually used and yet we have a report that talks about the various weapons and talks about assumptions that they were used, that they were used by paramilitaries or by other forces, and clearly is not referenced by Dr. Baccard and does not appear to be part of his conclusions or findings. But it's a fairly bulky exhibit that we have being proposed by the Office of the Prosecutor, and again it's not authored by Dr. Baccard, it's authored by Franck Pages. I believe the original is in French, is part of the French forensic mission. And it's -- respectfully, it's the opinion of myself and some of the other teams that this exhibit ought not to come into evidence in this form through Dr. Baccard, who I don't think can speak to some of the matters that are asserted and give information as to what bases there are for the impermissible assumptions and assertions that are made therein. And, again, I don't know whether this is something that the Prosecution intends to rely on, but it is listed in the 65 ter notification of exhibits that they intended to lead with this witness, and so that's why I raise it. And that would be my final preliminary point on this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Stamp, your position on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution does intend to rely upon that exhibit. Some of the conclusions of Dr. Baccard, including his affirmation of the conclusions of the French experts, to some degree, relies or rely upon matters contained in that particular exhibit. It is not uncommon; indeed, it is to be submitted that it is proper for a forensic scientist to obtain from various subspecialties, for example, ballistics, areas of analysis that might assist in the consideration of the evidence before them, which is exactly what happened here. One of Dr. Baccard's areas of specialty, if you look at his curriculum vitae, is an area of what is called wound ballistics. That is an area of science where you can examine a wound and relate it to the type of weapons. And in those circumstances, it would be appropriate for a ballistic -- for a pathologist to review a ballistic report to see if they are assisted in making the findings or if they, in any way, compromise whatever scientific findings can be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This sounds like it's a matter we'll have to deal with when it arises. It may be that Dr. Baccard refers to it to identify conclusions which he is making, but of course the report itself will have to be established in some way. And when we come to address these issues, we'll see whether it's satisfactorily compiled for the purpose for which you intend to use it or not. So let's wait until that arises. No doubt our attention will be drawn to it by Mr. Ivetic when it does. We'll probably reserve the question at that stage until we get to the end of the cross-examination and make a determination on how much it has assisted our consideration of Dr. Baccard's evidence at that stage. Now, that appears to clear the deck, so let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which language do you wish to use in the course of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask to be able to speak my mother tongue, i.e., French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you speak the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Could you start by stating your name and your present occupation.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: My name is Eric Baccard. I am currently the coordinator of forensic and criminologist activities at the office of the prosecutor of the ICC.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And by profession you are what? Could you say?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 31st of January, 2002, where were you employed and in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: On the 31st of January, 2002, well, I can't tell you with any certainty, but I believe that I was at the time employed as a chief forensic pathologist of the OTP of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in that capacity, did you prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I prepared a report, but it took me several months to prepare that report. It took me from six to seven months. I started in 2001 and I finished when I filed the report in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 31st of January, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the material that the report covered? What is the topic of the report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: This report dealt with forensic examinations, examinations of bodies, of autopsies, crime scene investigations also conducted by several forensic teams that worked in Kosovo in the year 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the report is Exhibit 1809, P1809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This will be admitted, Mr. Stamp, subject to the exclusion of the parts that you and Mr. Ivetic will agree upon between now and Wednesday relating to areas which are not the subject of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Could we go immediately to page 81 -- 82 -- 81 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I imagine that just for the sake of clarification, I imagine that means we are marking that for identification, on the basis we'll make the final decision on admission when we see your agreed confirmation of what's to be excluded from our consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Pages 80 to 81 consist of your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I see here, apart from various work and scholarship in forensic pathology, toxicology, medical law, criminalistics, forensic psychiatry, you also have at least two degrees in wound ballistics.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I hold only one degree in wound ballistics. These are studies I did at the Faculty of Medicine in Marseilles. I also hold a diploma in criminology after studying at the Faculty of Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes, one degree in wound ballistics. But you're also an expert of the court of appeal in Grenoble in wound ballistics, forensic pathology and forensic anthropology; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I'm an expert with the court of appeal, but I'm, most importantly, a national expert with the cour de cassation, the supreme court we have in France. With regard to forensic anthropology, I have training but I don't have a degree in that specific area of forensic anthropology.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're also president of the French Wound Ballistics Society.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I was the president of that society, because this report is quite old now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you testify in respect to the matters stated in your report in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic on the 21st of May, 2002? And in that testimony, did you clarify certain aspects of your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I testified during two days in May 2002. I also testified at another date. I do not remember whether that was in June or July 2002, and I testified on that particular date about another site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if you just give me a moment. Dr. Baccard, we've been given the report you did in relation to the 1999 investigations, and you've just been referred to the curriculum vitae that's in that report. Your life has moved on since then. We already know that you're now chief of the same subject matter but at the ICC. I think we would like to have your CV updated. We'll have a break for about half an hour later on this morning, and rather than try to get you to remember anything significant that's occurred since you gave evidence in the Milosevic trial, it might be helpful if you just took five minutes during that break to think it through and give us a completed update on your CV when you return after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- a copy exists, but I had thought that there was no difference between this updated CV, curriculum vitae, except that he was now at the ICC. However, there might be a difference. But we do have a copy ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: ... which was done this year. So perhaps you could upload that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I see the copy you have just now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. The only difference since the previous resume was drafted is the fact that I now work for the ICC since October 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In 2002, when you completed the report and then gave evidence, were you a full-time employee of the OTP here or were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never been employed full time, Your Honour. I worked on a contract basis. On several occasions, and after 2002, I continued working as a forensic consultant for the OTP; this was still on a contract basis and I was monitoring the post mortem examinations in Macedonia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Earlier this morning when you were asked your current post, you said that you were the chief pathologist -- sorry, you were the coordinator of forensic and criminologist activities at the OTP of the ICC. Is your role there similar to the one you had here? Is it a consultancy position or are you there fully engaged on the work of the ICC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I currently work full time since October of 2004 for the OTP at the ICC. And what I do goes beyond forensic and criminal activities because I'm also in charge of monitoring the work of the geographical systems and satellite imaging systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Between 31st January 2002 and October 2004, is there any other significant development in your career that we should be aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except for the fact that I have worked for the OTP at the ICTY on several occasions, I also worked as an expert in France and I worked for various domestic jurisdictions in France, whether these be civilian or criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I see here that you were a scientific consultant of the European Institute of Forensic Medicine during that period I've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I think this should be uploaded into the system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you should then alert us to the number that it has and we will admit it, because it does advance our knowledge of Dr. Baccard's experience. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that you did testify on the 20 -- you testified in the Milosevic case twice - may I just remind you of the dates - the first time being the 21st of May, 2002, and the next time on the 15th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As far as my first testimony is concerned, if I remember correctly, the testimony lasted two days, the 21st and 22nd of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the first occasion you testified in respect to the matters in your report of January 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you prepare another report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's also correct, Prosecutor. The OTP - I believe it was Mr. Dirk Ryneveld - has asked me on the 22nd of January, 2002 -- gave me documents which contained a report conducted by French forensic scientists, and this was the first time that I got to know about this report on a site which I did not know anything about. This was an added as an addendum to my report afterwards. This report pertains to -- this was a post mortem report conducted by Professors Lecomte and Vorhauer as well as a crime scene investigation report. This concerned the Cirez site which had been investigated on the 2nd and 3rd of July, 1999, by the French forensic team of experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your report is dated the 23rd of May, 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: This was on the 23rd of May. According to the copy I have, this was on the 23rd of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the addendum report is entered as P384. I think it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The transcript for the 21st and the 22nd of May is P2747. I think they've all been uploaded into e-court in one sequential bundle, so for the 21st and the 22nd of May and the 15th of July, it's 2747, P2747.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I imagine the order in respect to the section not related to his evidence here applies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript will be marked for identification on the same basis as the original report. The supplementary report, though, can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go first to your initial report. We see from the report that it analyses various other reports by forensic scientists who did investigation in Kosovo in 1999. Firstly, just for clarity, did you participate in those investigations in the field in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: My answer is no. In 1999 I worked for the ICTY. I was in Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We can see from your report that these field investigations were done by a variety of international teams. Were the methodologies applied by these teams consistent or were they different in some cases?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The purpose of the assignment I had been given by Mr. Dirk Ryneveld was as follows: We had to analyse the protocols, procedures, and methodologies observed by the various teams on the ground, and admittedly some of these teams sometimes came up with different findings. The overall conclusion was to state that these discrepancies in no way affected the conclusions that had been drawn on the basis of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the -- before I proceed to that, did you also review or check the professional qualifications of the scientific experts who did these reports in the field in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor. Automatically we always checked the qualifications for our colleagues. And if you would like me to expand on this, I can say that these forensic teams were, generally speaking, made up of forensic pathologists who, generally speaking, headed a forensic institute in their home country. These people were well known in their country and internationally also these people had written a number of articles, and their professional qualifications met the requirements we expected for that kind of assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which takes me to the next question. In respect to all of the material that you used for your report, did the standard of forensic science apply much, the standard which is appropriate in international forensic science?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. These criteria were the same as the criteria which were used internationally. As I mentioned -- as I have mentioned already, there were a number of differences that were due, for instance, to the fact that some people used X-rays and other people didn't, and in certain cases the British team, for instance, the British team did not look into internal organs when conducting their forensic examination but conducted an external examination and used X-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you find in respect to any of the reports for the various sites that the discrepancies or errors that you observed would have affected the overall findings in those reports?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I think these reports need to be put into perspective. These were conducted in 1999, and at the time this was done with what was available. These were emergency situations. This had to be prepared hurriedly. We did not have well-equipped autopsy rooms. Sometimes post mortem examinations had to be conducted against a -- with just a door that had been put on pieces of wood. Sometimes we had no water at all. This is just to say that, given the number of victims that we examined, some errors were discovered in the reports afterwards. On reading the report again, I did discover some errors when I compared photo albums, for instance, and some of the descriptions contained in the reports. A list of all of this has been drawn up and are contained in the annexes to the reports. These annexes can be found at the end of my summary report, but I will say that these discrepancies were minor discrepancies and did not in any way question the diagnosis which had been made on the type of wound or the cause of death. These were minor mistakes which did not question the general conclusions which my colleagues had come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Before we move to the individual sites, can I ask you one or two general questions. These autopsies were generally performed some two or three months after the persons were killed and many of these bodies were exhumed. Can you just expand briefly, if you can, on the area of your report that is entitled "Status of the Body." What difficulties in particular does the fact that many of these bodies were skeletonised, partially or fully decomposed, many of them were burnt, what challenges would these present to the person who conducted these forensic examinations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have an objection to the first part of that question, that is to say, the sentence dealing with "these autopsies were generally performed some two or three months after the persons were killed and many of these bodies were exhumed." I think to ask the question that way doesn't really provide a foundation for knowledge of when these individuals or corpses were deceased. And in any event, I believe that the doctor will rightly not be able to -- in his profession I believe there's always a suggestion or an indication of a particular time-period, but depending on the circumstances it may not be able to be tied down as specifically as counsel is indicating. And to make a broad statement covering these many sites in that manner, I think, misstates the evidence that the doctor has presented in his report and that I expect he will present here. And I think if the question is based upon that kind of assertion, there's a lack of foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you mean to be that specific, Mr. Stamp, or were you simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I could make it a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You're not suggesting that the period is one of two or three months specifically, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It varies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All you're saying is that because of the passage of time and the effect of the earth upon the bodies and indeed in some instances fire, it made forensic examination more challenging that it might otherwise have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're asking for the doctor's comments on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you deal with that, please, Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You did sum it up appropriately. The forensic doctor and the expert, in general terms, comes up against greater difficulty as time passes and the victim has died a longer while ago. What we do have available to us, data which can be less and less used because a body deteriorates over time, and it is easy to state a number of things when the body is a fresh body. The post mortem examination will be more difficult when we are faced with a putrified body. There are several stages in the putrifaction process, and with increasing difficulty we will have to deal with mummified bodies; in other words, bodies where the skin has been dehydrated and there's only the skin left. Greater difficulties are encountered when we are faced with bodies which have been skeletonised, where there are no soft tissues left anymore, and we are left with the sole skeleton. We also run into serious difficulties when we are faced with what we call body parts or remains, parts of the body which have been partially destroyed by fire, for instance. And it is easy to understand that if we are faced with a wound in the abdomen, that the wound has altered the organs and the muscular mass and has not affected the skeleton, that is one thing. When you have a skeletonised corpse, i.e., a skeleton, you will find no trace whatsoever on the victim. In that case you have to use whole sways of arguments and draw conclusions from the immediate vicinity; namely, you have to look at clothing, you have to look at defects on the clothes, like holes in the clothes. For instance, if a projectile has gone through the clothing, these holes can be surrounded by a bloodstain which can confirm not only that this is rather typical, that there has been a wound and that the wound has bled, and one can also closer to the skeleton find deformed projectiles. And all of this has to be put together, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could, Doctor, turn to your report dealing with the Bela Crkva area. That is page 27.

utterances.text: There are one or two questions in respect to that report which I would like to ask you very quickly, Dr. Baccard. And if we look through the report, we see at various places that the medical examiner described the condition of burnt, partly skeletonised body fragments and, for example, at page 2, says that the chin portion configuration is consistent with that of an adult female. "In respect to bone cluster 4, he says a gracile morphology of the cranial fragments indicate the remains to represent an adult female." How, in circumstances where, as in this case, burnt body fragments are recovered, is the determination of sex made?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: My answer will be of a general nature. Yes, it is possible indeed, depending on the kind of bone you find, it is possible to determine the gender of the victim. On an anthropological -- forensic anthropological basis, some part of the anatomy have a great significance when determining the gender. I'm thinking in particular of the cranium, in particular the basis of cranium. And as you quite rightly said, the chin, the angle of the chin is very useful as well. What can also help to determine the gender are the bones of the pelvis. That can give a very good indication when it comes to gender. Apart from these types of bones that can help determine the gender, there are other factors that are taken into account with less significance. It's the robustness of the bones, of the thigh bone, et cetera. You can also base your determination on the examination of the teeth; that can give you some indication about gender. But the main parts of bones that can help you to render a conclusion are the pelvis and the cranium, and the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And briefly, the examiners found the body parts of at least 12 children.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without going through the various examples given in the report itself, how, generally speaking, is this determination made? I imagine, of course, that the size of the bones, but sometimes you might have small adults or large children, relatively. What can you say about how age is determined when you find body parts in this condition?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: When it comes to the bones, apart from the size of the bones, that can be very misleading because you have adults who are very small and some children who, on the other hand, are very, very tall. So what you do is you look at the cartilage, the level of articulation, for example. And when you look at the various parts of the bones, you can determine the age, the fusion level of the bones; you can determine the age that -- with a good significance. Statistically speaking, the articular places are very significant at the skull level. The interior part of the clavicle, of the ribs, especially of the fourth rib, some bones of the pelvis, some bones of the wrist are very significant. And with all this you can try to determine the age of the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD

So in that particular instance, they were confronted with a lot of problems because these bodies were skeletonised, first of all; secondly, these bones had been partially burned; and thirdly, animals had bitten parts of these bones -- gnawed at these bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible animals could have moved the fragments within the house?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP

utterances.text: No, Prosecutor. I noted this discrepancy when I testified in the Milosevic trial. utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on quickly to the Izbica site. This site presented quite a significant amount of difficulties because of the paucity of material you had to work on. And you did in your report at 2.7.5 - and that's page 44 - indicate that the cause of death was very difficult to determine having regard to the material. And further, you indicated that there were limitations to your observations made in respect of the video and the photographs. I'd like to ask you this, however: In respect to the findings that some persons were shot at close range because of the marks of a twin or burning or muzzle marks on the skin, the findings that they were shot at close range can be given with reasonable scientific certainty.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. The Izbica case is a difficult one. You were on a -- insofar as the work conducted by the forensic French medical team came up against the fact that there are very few body remains left. And they did find clothes and body remains, but on the basis of the body remains one could not find any traces of wounds. But some of the clothing did contain defects which would be consistent with holes made by gun-shots. Some of the edges of these holes were burnt, which led some ballistic expert to say that the shot had been fired at short range. That's the first point. Second point is that alongside these direct-examination reports conducted on the crime sites I was given a videotape, and on this videotape there were shots of a series of victims on which a number of findings could be made. Of course, these were not shots for scientific purposes. These were limited in material because the victims were lying on their backs and they were all dressed. And only certain anatomical parts of the body could be seen, and some of the shots were sometimes blurred and were photographed from quite a distance, and the wounds could not be measured in any way. So to sum up, only some of the photographs could be interpreted from a forensic point of view. The third point I wanted to make was this was only an analysis of documents and video pictures. This can in no way replace examination conducted on the victim or post mortem examination. This has a limited value. That said, I was able to state two things. Firstly, this videotape seemed to be authentic and true to fact because some of the details that could be seen there is not something you could make up; things like putrifaction phenomena or the way the bodies were placed, the victims were placed. And all this was consistent and seemed sincere because I did think that maybe some of this had been staged or maybe it was fake. Also, in addition, on some of these shots you could see wounds which were consistent with -- I never used the word "certainty" in my report. I just said one or other shot or picture was consistent with wounds that could be caused by a gun-shot. Some could be caused by fire-arms; some could be areas where the print of the muzzle of the weapon could be seen. Other cases there were charred remains on the edge, and in other instances, traces of powder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect of those cases that you referred to in your report where there were ballistics burn marks on the clothing or on the skin, could the -- or is the finding that these persons were shot from close range, is that a finding that is scientific and sustainable, in your view, notwithstanding the paucity of evidence otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I'm unable to answer this question directly because these finding were made by the experts. And the clothing was not made available to me so I was unavailable to examine the latter. I had no access to the photographs and was therefore unable to conduct a second examination. What I can say, however, is that these findings were made by experts who are well-known and well-reputed experts in their own country. They are used to these type of examinations, and I have no reason to question their findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP

utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have some specificity. I believe there's actually two; one contained within the autopsy section itself that relates to wound ballistics and one which relates to a different type of ballistics. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain a little bit further. What's -- I read it here at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- just a second. Mr. Ivetic, whether it's "and" or "or" doesn't really seem to matter here, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There were four Kacanik sites. The first one we could look at is Kotlina, and that's at page 49 of the report -- 48 of the report. utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD

Page 42 lists evidence that was recovered -- could I ask you this: It is a common thing in forensic examination to send off artefacts recovered for further chemical or scientific examination; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of the page, you will see that some of the recovered evidence at 5 was "fire debris from shaft wall of upper well; 6, clothing remnants to be investigated for traces of incendiary or explosive material." And if we go to page 88 of the same exhibit, we see in the middle of the page: "Material submitted for examination: Samples 5, 6, and 19," corresponding to those we just looked at. Traces of TNT in sample 5 could not be ruled out." Doctor, is this methodology an approach, an approach as standard and proper method of examining fragments that have been recovered from a crime scene, fragments of various materials or artefacts?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Prosecutor, first of all, I'm discovering for the first time the findings of this examination, and as you can see on reading my report, this had not been given to me. As far as your question is concerned, i.e., whether it is customary to give this kind of artefact to a qualified laboratory so that one can detect traces of explosives, this is, of course, part and parcel of a complete examination when a crime scene investigation is conducted and forensic examination is conducted. To be more specific, as far as the methods are concerned, I'm not an expert in explosives, and in chemistry, not either. I have some knowledge, general knowledge, of which kinds of methods I use and spectrometry mass-spectrometry and chromatography in gaseous phase are standard methods used when this kind of analysis is conducted. But as I'm not an expert, I cannot expand on this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What I was asking, I think you've answered that. It is acceptable practice for a forensic scientist to send away material like that to be examined by a chemist or an expert in that field.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.text: Could we go to the front page of 361. First page, please. Could you go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the top box, it says: "Crime Scene Group II 1999 Kosovo." Is that the report you received?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The report, as it is, contains the autopsies that I showed you, but it also contains a record of the material collected and the submission for chemical examination. You said you did not review that record. Am I to understand that in this case you reviewed as source material the autopsy reports but you did not review the documentation in respect to the submission of the artefacts for chemical analysis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I must say that during the break I tried to recollect this particular case - this goes back four years already - and my answer is not quite certain as it was before. It is possible that the results of these chemical analyses were shown to me, but because of my particular background, of my profession, I dealt mostly with what was within my field of expertise, i.e., the autopsy reports. I cannot say with any certainty whether the results of the chemical analysis were to be found in the report that was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only indicate to the Court that the report of the chemical analysis forms part of the overall document. It's a pretty long document, and the submission for analysis is at the back of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The submission for analysis is one thing, but you also have the result of the analysis, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how does it affect the conclusion on page 51 of Dr. Baccard's report? And it may indeed -- because it's -- it extends over all the Kacanik cases, does it, and therefore -- or is it only this section of Kacanik --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Kotlina, only Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only Kotlina. So how does it affect the conclusion at 2.9.5?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It confirms the conclusion to the degree that where the conclusion refers to 84 per cent of the victims, the cause of death is relating to explosives. But more than that, it confirms the evidence of Hazbi Loku, who testified in the case, that he saw the men being thrown in the wells, some being shot, and that when they were in the wells, explosives were thrown in. I believe at the time he testified there was some issue raised as to whether or not he saw what he said he saw and whether or not explosives were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the removal of doubt may be achieved by agreement. Again, this is a matter we would invite you and Mr. Ivetic to consider, and it may be that agreement can be reached and you do not have the difficulty of establishing by extraneous means the views expressed following the chemical analysis. But in view of the doubt that Dr. Baccard has expressed about whether he saw the results, then it would do us well to overcome any possible lacuna by agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to add something. In my report, I mention the diagnosis, the conclusions, based on the autopsies and on the external examination, but also based on the presence of shrapnels. But I did not refer to anything being confirmed by chemical analysis. It's something new that I discover now. But in any case, if you look at my colleagues' reports, the anatomical injuries and the shrapnels were sufficient to confirm the diagnosis of death caused by an explosion, by explosives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we move on to Dubrava. Your Honours, I see here in respect to Dubrava and the remaining crime scenes that what we have are pretty straightforward exhumation reports and autopsies. Unless the Court is of the view that I should go through the autopsies, it is probably not a matter that needs to be taken now. For Dubrava, there are two exhumation reports, P370 and P371, followed by the autopsy reports in respect to identified persons in the schedules of the indictment. Similarly, if one follows the notification in the Vata Slatina case, the situation remains the same. In Stagovo, there is another report by the Swiss Disaster Victim Identification Team, and it includes the autopsies in respect to the named individuals in the indictment. I don't think it's necessary to go through these autopsies. What I could do, Your Honours, if it is convenient to the Court, is file or present to the Court a schedule with the relevant pages, because I think one or two of these reports are very long and the gravamen of the autopsies are located in a narrow range of pages but scattered in the report. In other words, there are many photographs, there are pictures of delta structures, et cetera, in the report followed by the autopsies in respect of -- there's a narrative of the autopsies in respect to the individual victims. So I would proceed that way, having regard to what was indicated by the Court earlier, unless the Court thinks it is convenient to proceed through the individual autopsies now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't require you to do that, Mr. Stamp, but we do require you to identify the exhibits to which the witness is referring or upon which he has relied in respect of each section.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where you -- I don't mean at this minute, but it would have been helpful if a list was already available which identified the pages where you've indicated that there's a lengthy report and we need only refer to certain parts of it. Now, hopefully, along with the exercise that you and Mr. Ivetic are to engage in by Wednesday, you'll be able to give us a list of exhibits to which this report refers, along with a restriction to the pages that are relevant to the issues that we have to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I note one other matter. Are you continuing with the examination or have you reached the end of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Two matters I want to cover very briefly in respect to Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You deal with the site Gornja Sudimlja, in the municipality of Vucitrn, at page 67. I see that in the Milosevic case, at page 5263, you said that as a general rule you would be able to independently detect even an error as to the cause of death from the material furnished. If we look at appendix 7, at page 149. I think if we can go to page 147, not 149. Now, at case C16, third from the bottom, you say, in conclusion, the cause of death in respect to this person is not "the thoracic wound because the shot was very tangential and superficial. It is not a penetrating shot. The cause of death is skull/brain injury." Now, is that a situation where you could, as a result of your expertise and examination material provided, come to your own conclusion with respect to cause of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. When you have a description of both wounds and when you have the relevant pictures available to you, it's quite possible to say that the thoracic wound did not cause any lesion in vital organs and that the cause of death is related to the skull/brain injury that was accompanied with irreversible lesions, for example, injury to the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to that site, you found a significant amount of discrepancies or errors. Did these errors in any way affect the overall conclusions, particularly that most of the victims or a significant amount of the victims had been shot in the back?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No -- yes, you're right. When I looked at the documents that were available and the photographs as well, I was able to identify a number of discrepancies. But once I had taken note of these discrepancies, and taking these discrepancies into account, I can say that the overall conclusion remained valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I referred you to one overall conclusion about them being shot in the back. Is also another important conclusion at page 67, 2.12.6.4, where you say: "The majority of the wounds at the level of the trunk, abdominal/thoracic region, that's 58 per cent, and at the level of head and neck, cervical/cephalic region, 37 per cent. No case of gun-shot injury was found concerning the lower limbs, and a few has been done to the upper limbs, 5 per cent. These findings must be interpreted with the circumstances of the firing." I take it also that these findings are not affected by the discrepancies that you observed.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, because the percentages, the figures that I give, are figures that I have computed myself based on all the information available to me and taking into account all the discrepancies that I identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. In respect to the Suva Reka site, this, again, was an exhumation of a burial ground that had already been exhumed of the bodies. Or may I put it this way: There were just two identifiable bodies, in your view. Can you explain or expand on the reasons why there were only two identifiable bodies.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I read the material that was given to me, various anthropological reports prepared by Dr. Black, the autopsy report of Dr. Milewski, the anthropological report of Dr. Black prepared at another date, and so on and so forth, and when reading these reports I identified a number of discrepancies. Because the description of some of the clusters of human remains did not add up, because of these discrepancies, I decided to leave aside that which was doubtful and only take into account and retain what I could find in every one of the reports and that would not -- and that would not be a cause for confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And as a result you have only listed cause of death in respect to Faton Berisha and Fatime Berisha.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because as for the other human remains, they were in such a state, they were commingled and there was no lesion to be found on any of these human remains that could have enabled us to determine the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I indicated, Your Honours, the report in respect to Cirez, the eight women found in Cirez, is already in evidence and speaks for itself. That is P383. I have nothing further in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be, I think, Mr. Stamp, that you haven't, in relation to the transcript, asked the normal questions about whether the witness, subject to the amendment that you did go into, would give that evidence today if he were asked the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I did not? Well, I should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the occasions when you testified in the Milosevic trial, did you answer truthfully to the questions you were asked to the extent that if you were asked again, would your answers remain the same?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Of course, sir. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I also indicate before I sit that the updated CV is in the system at P2784.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll follow the order of the indictment, and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I have questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Baccard. My name is Tomislav Visnjic. I am General Ojdanic's Defence counsel and I have a few questions for you. Like any layperson, I'm going to put a few general questions to you. So could you please give me answers in order for me to lay a foundation for some other questions that I wish to put to you after that. Is it correct, Doctor, that the distance of firing a bullet is established on the basis of the traces of gunpowder of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. A number of criterion enable one to establish the distance at which it was fired, but it's not the only criterion. There can also be traces which have to do with ammunition constituents. In the case of certain projectiles or filling material, like polystyrene and lesions which are connected to the gas, for instance, some lesions have nothing to do with powder traces. There can be just tears in the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So in addition -- thank you. So in addition to the powder traces that would consist of particles that have not burned and traces of metal and precisely what you referred to in your answer, those would be the elements on the basis of which we could establish what the distance of the fired bullet is; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to repeat the ammunition constituents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, just a moment. Dr. Baccard, could you repeat what you said about the constituents of the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. I said that notwithstanding powder traces, powder traces is part of ammunition, but there are other things that can be taken into account. The stuffing which is part of a projectile, or if it's a multiple projectile, in addition to the powder there can be a filling material for certain kinds of American projectiles which are not powder but which stabilise these elements. This is projected into the air when the shot is fired. In the case of pressed, short-range shots, we have characteristic lesions which are connected to the expansion of the gas under the skin which cause torn wounds, without one being able to find any traces of gunpowder. So a powder projection are part and parcel of what enable us to establish the firing range, but this is not the only factor to be borne in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that absolute proximity or immediate proximity means that the barrel of a hand-held weapon was, when the firing occurred, leaning on an object or a body part or was a few millimetres away from it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that relative or indirect proximity means that the barrel of a hand-held weapon was, during firing, removed from a body or from clothing at a distance of about 15 or 20 centimetres for modern pistols, 50 to 70 centimetres in the case of revolvers, and 1 to 1.5 metres for rifles?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The answer is no. I don't know if the translation is accurate, but the firing range, what you mentioned would be more in line with short range and not long range.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The question had to do with relative proximity or indirect proximity or range.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I think we need to specify here that the subdivisions are purely theoretical. They rely on a number of factors; namely, the type of weapon, the length of the barrel, the powder load, and a number of factors which you mentioned, i.e., if there are clothing in the way. I'm talking about residues, of course, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we proceed to the next question, I suspect it is going to be -- it's corrected. There was an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in all cases where traces are not found, ballistics experts and forensic experts agree that the projectile was fired from a distance?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The answer can't be categorical because other factors could be borne in mind. The weather conditions, for instance, if it has rained, smoke residues can be washed away; and if there is an intermediary target, like a screen or clothing, if such a thing exists there, we sometimes cannot find traces on the body itself. So I think one has to bear in mind these factors and one cannot answer categorically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: These factors that you mentioned, in actual fact they can only lead to a more conservative interpretation of distance, the distance from which a bullet had been fired. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't understand the word you use, "conservative."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to deal with it this way: According to the methodology that you use, what would be a mean distance to establish whether a rifle had been fired from close range?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but once again I cannot answer categorically. The length of the barrel, whether at the extreme end of the barrel there is a special mechanism which can be a sound muffler, for instance, or a flash-hiding system, or if the quantity of powder is more or less great and weather conditions, all these factors must be taken into account when you consider smoke residues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are there any standards in literature regarding the distance which can be established?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The answer is no. Arms ammunition experts, when they calculate a firing shot in numbers, conduct comparative shots using the same weapon whenever it's possible or a similar type of weapon; and if possible, they use munitions that are part of the same batch. And if they're not part of the same batch and not available, then a similar munition is used. This is needed if we are to provide figures. We then have to conduct comparative shootings; otherwise, all of this remains rather approximate, whether it's an intermediary shot, contact range, short range, long range. This, of course, depends on the type of weapon used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, now I'm going to ask you about the work of the French team, or rather, the French mission in 1999. Do you know what method they used to establish the range involved and what parameters they used for establishing the range at which a bullet had been fired when they wrote this analysis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Are you referring to a particular case or is this a general question you are putting to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a specific report. Gornja Sudimlja, for instance.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As far as firing range is concerned, what you find in the report in question depends on whether marks of burns have been found on the clothing, whether powder traces have been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, it was my understanding on the basis of the evidence you gave in the Milosevic case that you were not responsible for the work of the French mission in 1999. You assumed responsibility for the work of these teams only in the year 2000. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Nonetheless, at one point, as far as what I did in the year 2000, I was not in charge of the French mission, I was in charge of the purely disciplinary and international teams that were set up by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. This included experts from different countries. There were not only French experts on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that on decaying bodies one cannot establish exactly at what range the bullet had been fired?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As a rule, it is very difficult because of the transudation phenomenon which you find on the skin and the peeling off of the skin, when the epidermis will flake off. This, nonetheless, can be determined by looking at clothes of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Doctor, that perhaps one can establish that a bullet had been fired from absolute range when we can see on the flat bones of the body that there had been smears with black substance in a situation when a body is already decaying or had already decayed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As far as contact range is concerned, you can have a tattooed area which is not on the skin itself but which is located on the external part of the underlying bone. In that case, this tattooed area which is tattooed with powder will be protected by the skin, and it's on the external side of the bone that you will find embedded powder on the outside of the skin -- of the bone. Other clinical signs can be observed. For instance, the print of the muzzle of the weapon, the mine chamber under the skin, and a widening of the hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Am I right if I say that, according to your report, 2.12.3, that is, all the corpses found in Gornja Sudimlja had decayed/decomposed, with the exception of two that are mentioned there specifically? 2.12.3.2, that is the reference.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Doctor, if I say that it is impossible only on the basis of what the exit/entry wound looks like that one can state what the calibre of the bullet involved was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: One has to be extremely cautious when doing this. You think it is one or other calibre, but there is no scientific comparison that can be drawn between a calibre and exit and entry wounds which has to do with the elasticity of the skin and the movement of the projectile and resistant factors of the various tissues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the reference you've just given, 2.12.3.2, I can't find in my copy, and I can see that in this section the numbers do jump around a little. Could it be under a different number in my copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I probably should have indicated that the numbers do jump around. That is why I tended to refer to the numbers as the page number and the paragraph heading. I think it is "Status of Bodies" at the bottom of the page 2.12.5.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Point 5.2? That clarifies it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to what I have in translation, it should be on page 76 in a document -- in document 158, out of 158, but now my colleagues are telling me not to refer to it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On page 76?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Mr. Ivetic tells me now that I cannot rely on this piece of information because the pages in translation obviously do not correspond to the e-court pages. But I think that a reference to the paragraph will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in your copy the paragraph number is 2.12.3.2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the paragraph, and next to it I see it says in the original "2.12.5.2" to complicate things even further. It was probably first done in French, then translated into English where the numbers got mixed up, and then it was further translated, so all these problems arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Actually, I think there's a transposition of a 3 and a 5, but it's now been clarified for the moment. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my copy, which has been written in English, I have the same page numbering as Mr. Visnjic. In paragraph 2.12.2, "Status of the Bodies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2.12.3.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please take a look at Exhibit P334, a report from the French mission. I will put a question first and then I will ask you to look at two autopsy reports. The question is the following: On what basis is it claimed that the immediate proximity is equivalent to 50 centimetres, bearing in mind that we agreed a little while ago that absolute or immediate proximity is either the weapon against the skin or only a few millimetres away from the skin and the clothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we could see page 51 of Exhibit 334, which is a report for L11, C13.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: L1, C13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be a translation problem here, because the English says: "Fired at very short range." This was a French report, so -- is that correct or not, Mr. Visnjic? Is this a French report?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a French report, Your Honour, yes, and it is a matter of translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, do you have the original French version of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have the English version on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the French version is in the system. We could put it on the screen instead of the version in Serbian, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should, Mr. Visnjic, and let's see how it compares with the English translation, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put the French version on the screen. I think it's the same page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's identical, I think, to the English version. It talks about "a tres courte distance a 50 centimetres environ." So it's what I would say is identical to the English. Now, in Serbian, can we hear from you, Mr. Visnjic, what the equivalent sentence says in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the Serbian version, it says in the conclusion it's a 12-millimetre calibre bullet fired from an immediate proximity at a distance of about 2 centimetres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 50 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, please answer the question. That way we understand what the various languages are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, when you look at this autopsy report, on what basis was it concluded that the distance from which the bullet was fired was about 50 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I'm not the expert who conducted the post mortem examination; it is, therefore, difficult to say what material my colleague used to come up with this finding. According to what I read in this report, there was a weapons ammunition expert who was there at the time the post mortem examination was conducted and I think that his findings led to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in the description of this autopsy -- or in any document you reviewed, is there anything that can provide a basis for such conclusions and is that basis stated anywhere? This description consists of three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown pages 2 and 3 of this document, the next two pages, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In French, preferably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are pages 52 and 53 in French, I believe, 52 and 53. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We still have English, I'm afraid, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a version in French, a hard copy here, and I can hand it to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the same question refers to L2, 34. So if you could look at both autopsy reports, please. Doctor, in these two reports, is there any element on the basis of which we could conclude that the French team arrived at the conclusion that the bullet was fired at a distance of 50 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It is indicated on the screen that the distance is 50 centimetres. I think it would have been better for the expert to indicate that this shot was consistent with rather than providing a figure, i.e., the distance, which can only be ascertained when we know which kind of weapon and ammunition has been used. That said, we can figure out that it has been shot at close range; for instance, if there are blackish burns around the wound, this is an indication that the muzzle of the barrel of the weapon was very close to the skin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there such a finding in these two reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the L2, C34 report is concerned, in the thoracic region, it is specified that the entry wound is in the paramedian higher part of the thorax, 9 millimetres long, with blackish burns around the area in question. As far as the other report is concerned, L1, 13 -- L1, C13, it is specified that this was shot at short range, at 50 centimetres. But we don't have the information which the expert based his conclusions on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, this was a decaying body which had undergone putrifaction. We are now speaking of C34. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now look at another exhibit, P334 again, L1, C12.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please hand this to the witness, the French text, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, it says here that the bullet was fired from relatively close range, at a distance of about 2 metres -- less than 2 metres. Is there any basis for this conclusion in the report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I have not found any.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, now that we're talking about C12, the autopsy report L1, C12, it says that the calibre of the weapon is 5.45-5.56. Do you see here on what basis the calibre of the projectile was established?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I have found no indication of that in the expert report. I believe that this is something inferred from the entry wound, but this is something I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have already agreed that the calibre cannot be estimated from the entry wound scientifically; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, the answer is yes. I would certainly be more cautious when choosing my words. I would have used the word "consistent" and not been so 100 per cent sure. Once again, I was not there and I did not take part in the post mortem examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'm aware of this and that's why I asked you to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the doctor please be shown the same exhibit, but this time page 4. It's autopsy, or rather, excuse me, page 11, and the autopsy is L1, C3. I have the French version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in this autopsy report, no exit wound is mentioned on the body; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
